title: Shito
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: The cue is exact — the contents turn from deep red to very dark brown and the oil rises to the surface when the sauce is ready.
longDesc: Shito is the black chilli-and-dried-fish paste that sits beside everything in Ghana, and every household has its own recipe. This one is built on half a litre of oil, three red onions, three garlic cloves, eight ground guinea peppers, three inches of ginger and seventy-five grams of green kpakpo shito chillies with their seeds, then a hundred and twenty-five grams of chilli powder, fifty grams of dried prawn powder and fifty of crayfish or smoked fish powder. It cooks on low thirty to forty minutes, stirring almost continuously, until it turns from deep red to very dark brown and the oil rises.
ingredients: 500 ml rapeseed oil, or sunflower or vegetable oil, plus extra if required
7.5 cm piece fresh root ginger, finely grated
1 tbsp chopped thyme or rosemary leaves (optional)
75 g green kpakpo shito chillies, finely diced with the seeds — or green scotch bonnets, or 2 tbsp dried chilli flakes
50 g dried ground prawn or shrimp powder
50 g crayfish or smoked fish powder
steps: Fry the onions 2 to 3 minutes, until translucent.
Add the garlic, ground guinea peppers, ginger, the optional herb and the chillies, and fry a few minutes.
Stir in the tomato purée and the stock to make a thick paste.
Add the chilli powder and cook, stirring, 10 minutes.
Add the prawn and crayfish powders.
Cook on low 30 to 40 minutes, stirring almost continuously.
The contents should transform from deep red to very dark brown and the oil will rise to the surface when the sauce is ready.
Blend if you prefer it smooth.
Jar with about half an inch of oil on top. Keeps in the fridge up to a month.
chefTips: The colour change is the cue and it is unmistakable: deep red to very dark brown, with oil rising to the surface. Every documented shito gives the same endpoint in different words.
Stirring almost continuously for the last thirty to forty minutes. There is no way round it — the solids will catch and burn otherwise, and burnt shito is unsalvageable.
Half an inch of oil on top in the jar. That oil seal is what makes shito keep a month in the fridge, so do not skim it off.
Kpakpo shito chillies WITH THE SEEDS — the exclamation mark is hers. The seeds are a deliberate part of the heat.

A hundred and twenty-five grams of chilli powder is a great deal and it is this version's main heat source, rather than fresh scotch bonnets. A long-cook version uses seven scotch bonnets and no chilli powder at all.
Guinea peppers are grains of paradise. Eight, ground, is the printed amount.
Documented cooking times run from about fifty minutes to about three hours. This is the quick one; the long one is at GHA052 and tastes deeper.
commonMistakes: Stopping while it is still red.
Skimming the oil layer off before storing.
Rushing the final low simmer on higher heat.
sources: Adapted from 'Shito (Hot Pepper Sauce)', splendidtable.org, 17 July 2017, from Zoe's Ghana Kitchen (Mitchell Beazley, 2017). BYLINE: Zoe Adjonyoh. Yield as printed: 'Makes about 500 grams (1 lb 2 oz / 2 cups)'. Time as printed: '50 minutes cooking'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 500 ml (18fl oz) rapeseed oil, or substitute sunflower or vegetable oil, plus extra if required; 3 red onions, finely diced; 3 garlic cloves, very finely chopped; 8 guinea peppers, ground; 7.5 cm (3-inch) piece fresh root ginger, finely grated; 1 tablespoon chopped thyme or rosemary leaves (optional); 75 g (2 3/4 oz) green kpakpo shito chillies, finely diced (with seeds!), or substitute green Scotch Bonnets, or 2 tablespoons dried chilli flakes; 5–6 tablespoons tomato purée; 100 ml (3 1/2 oz) good-quality chicken stock; 125 g (4 1/2 oz) chilli powder; 50 g (1 3/4 oz) dried ground prawn or shrimp powder; 50 g (1 3/4 oz) crayfish or smoked fish powder; 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper; 1 teaspoon sea salt. The exclamation mark after 'with seeds' is as printed.

Method as printed: fry onions 2-3 min until translucent; add garlic, guinea peppers, ginger, herb and chillies and fry 'a few minutes'; stir in tomato purée and stock to a thick paste; add chilli powder and cook stirring 10 min; add prawn and crayfish powders, cook on low '30-40 minutes, stirring almost continuously'; optionally blend; jar with about ½ inch oil layer; fridge up to 1 month.
THE DONENESS CUE, verbatim and the best in the shito record: 'The contents should transform from deep red to very dark brown and the oil will rise to the surface when the sauce is ready.'
HEADNOTE, verbatim, and worth keeping because it frames every disagreement below: 'every household has its own recipe.'

THE THREE DOCUMENTED SHITOS DISAGREE ON ALMOST EVERYTHING EXCEPT THE CUE, recorded unreconciled. OIL: 500 ml here; 4 cups (Nadia Boachie, GHA052); 2 cups (Margaret Everitt). HEAT SOURCE: 125 g chilli powder and NO scotch bonnets here; 7 scotch bonnets and NO chilli powder (Boachie); 2 kpakpo plus 1 scotch bonnet (Everitt). COOK TIME: about 50 minutes here against about 3 hours (Boachie). Nothing is averaged.

A THIRD VERSION, recorded not published: Margaret Everitt as recipe contributor on kscuisine.com (site founder Kemi), originally 14 July 2014, republished 5 February 2020, TWO-PASS. Its ingredients: 4 large Onions; 2 cloves garlic; ½ cup Ground Crayfish; ½ cup Bonga fish; 3 Stock cubes; 2 Green kpakpo shito pepper or to taste; 1 Scotch bonnet as much as you can tolerate; 2 tablespoons Tomato Puree; 2 cups Oil; 3 inch Ginger. Its technique is distinctive — fry onions and ginger in the oil until brown, SIEVE THE OIL, then blend everything with the oil and no water — but IT GIVES NO ENDPOINT CUE, only 'The sauce starts to bubble. lower the heat at this point.' FLAG: its method says 'Wash the Shawa (dry fish)' while the ingredient list says 'Bonga fish', and both terms are Nigerian rather than Ghanaian.

A SOURCE REJECTED, named as requested: thefooddictator.com's 'The Hirshon Ghana Black Chili Sauce – Shito', byline 'The Generalissimo', 13 July 2018. It reads as a near copy of this recipe — the same 3 onions, 3 garlic, 7.5 cm ginger, 125 g chilli powder, 100 ml stock, and 8 'grains of paradise' for her 'guinea peppers' — with gochugaru and katsuobushi added. The byline is a persona, the second fetch was declined on copyright grounds so it is SINGLE-PASS, and it is unusable.

ON GUINEA PEPPERS: Aframomum melegueta, grains of paradise, a West African spice in the ginger family. The rejected source above renders them as 'grains of paradise', which confirms the identification.

ON KPAKPO SHITO: the small round Ghanaian chilli, aromatic and moderately hot; the source itself offers green scotch bonnets or dried chilli flakes as substitutes, which are hotter and less fragrant respectively.
storage: Up to a month refrigerated under its oil layer, per the author.
reheating: Not needed. Shito is served at room temperature or cold.
healthBenefits: Dried prawn and crayfish powders are very high in protein, calcium and iodine.
Capsaicin from the chilli has documented metabolic and analgesic activity.
Ginger and garlic both contribute anti-inflammatory compounds.
A small spoonful goes a long way, so the per-serving oil is modest.
culturalNote: A jar of shito travels with Ghanaians everywhere — it is the thing sent in suitcases to relatives abroad, and the thing a student takes to boarding school. That the headnote concedes every household has its own recipe is the honest position: the three documented versions share a colour change and a dried-shellfish base and almost nothing else.
